title: Letters, vowels and the marks of the mushaf
body: Arabic is written right to left in 28 consonant letters. Most letters join to the next one, so a letter changes shape at the start, middle or end of a word. Six letters never join forward: ا د ذ ر ز و.

Short vowels are written as marks. Fatḥa (a line above) gives a, kasra (a line below) gives i, and ḍamma (a small wāw above) gives u. A sukūn (a small circle) means the letter has no vowel. A shadda (a small w-shape) doubles the letter.

Tanwīn is a doubled vowel mark at the end of an indefinite noun, read -an, -in or -un. The Madani mushaf you will memorise also uses special marks. The dagger alif (ـٰـ) is a long ā that is not written as a full letter. The waṣla alif (ٱ) is silent when you join it to the word before. Small high letters and the pause marks (ۘ ۖ ۗ ۚ ۛ ۙ) tell you where you may stop.
points: Fatḥa a, kasra i, ḍamma u, sukūn no vowel, shadda doubles the letter.
Tanwīn (ـً ـٍ ـٌ) marks an indefinite noun.
ٱ (waṣla) is silent when joined to the word before; ـٰ is a long ā.
Pause marks: ۘ (mīm) you must stop, ۖ (ṣlā) better to continue, ۗ (qlā) better to stop, ۚ (jīm) either, ۛ (three dots) stop at one of the pair, never both; ۙ (lā) do not stop.

title: Noun, verb and particle
body: Arabic grammarians divide every word into three kinds. An ism (noun) names a thing or quality, and includes adjectives, pronouns and participles. A fiʿl (verb) shows an action tied to a time. A ḥarf (particle) only has meaning together with other words: prepositions, conjunctions, negatives and the like.

Signs of a noun: it can take al-, tanwīn, a preposition before it, or the genitive case. Signs of a verb: it can take qad, sa- or sawfa, or the past-tense endings such as -tu and -at. A particle takes none of these.
points: Ism: takes al-, tanwīn, a preposition or the genitive case.
Fiʿl: takes qad, sa-, sawfa, -tu, -at.
Ḥarf: takes none of the signs of a noun or a verb.
Pronouns, participles and maṣdars are all nouns.

title: Roots and patterns
body: Most Arabic words come from a root of three consonants that carries a core meaning. ك ت ب is about writing, so it gives kataba (he wrote), kitāb (book), kātib (writer) and maktūb (written).

A pattern (wazn) pours the root into a fixed shape, and each shape adds its own kind of meaning. Grammarians write patterns with ف ع ل standing for the three root letters: fāʿil is the doer, mafʿūl the thing done, and fiʿāl often a noun.

Learn a root once and you can read its family across the whole Quran. ر ح م gives raḥmān, raḥīm, raḥma and arḥām; ع ل م gives ʿilm, ʿalīm, ʿālamīn and ʿallama. The Roots tab shows every family with its count.
points: Root = the consonants that carry the meaning; pattern = the shape that adds the role.
Patterns are written with ف ع ل: fāʿil, mafʿūl, faʿīl, fiʿāl…
To find the root, strip prefixes, suffixes and the pattern's added letters (ا، و، ي، م، ت، ن، س).
The Roots tab lists every root in the Quran with its whole family.

title: The definite article and tanwīn
body: al- (ٱلْ) makes a noun definite, like 'the'. Before a 'sun letter' (ت ث د ذ ر ز س ش ص ض ط ظ ل ن) the lām is not pronounced and the next letter is doubled, as in ٱلرَّحْمَـٰنِ ar-raḥmān. Before a 'moon letter' the lām is heard, as in ٱلْحَمْدُ al-ḥamd.
A noun with tanwīn is indefinite, like 'a/an': كِتَـٰبٌ 'a book', هُدًى 'a guidance'. A noun is also definite when it is a proper name, a pronoun, or the first term of an iḍāfa (Lesson 9).
points: ٱلْ = definite; tanwīn = indefinite.
Sun letters absorb the lām of al-: ٱلشَّمْسِ ash-shams.
Moon letters keep it: ٱلْقَمَرِ al-qamar.
A noun never has both al- and tanwīn.

title: Gender
body: Every Arabic noun is masculine or feminine, and verbs, adjectives and pronouns agree with it. The commonest feminine sign is tāʾ marbūṭa (ة), as in رَحْمَة raḥma (mercy) and جَنَّة janna (garden). Others are a final alif maqṣūra (ـى) or alif mamdūda (ـاء), as in ذِكْرَى dhikrā.
Some nouns are feminine without any sign: أَرْض arḍ (earth), شَمْس shams (sun), نَفْس nafs (soul), نَار nār (fire). Broken plurals of things are treated as feminine singular for agreement.
points: ة, ـى and ـاء usually mark the feminine.
Feminine with no sign: arḍ, shams, nafs, nār, dār, yad.
Adjectives agree in gender with their noun.
Plurals of non-humans take feminine singular agreement.

title: Singular, dual and plural
body: Arabic counts in three numbers. The dual adds ـَانِ in the nominative or ـَيْنِ otherwise: جَنَّتَانِ 'two gardens'. The sound masculine plural adds ـُونَ or ـِينَ: مُؤْمِنُونَ, مُتَّقِينَ. The sound feminine plural adds ـَات: مُؤْمِنَات.

Most plurals are 'broken': the vowels inside the word change, as in كِتَاب → كُتُب and رَسُول → رُسُل. They have to be learned word by word, which is why the vocabulary trainer shows them as separate lemmas.
points: Dual: ـَانِ (nominative) / ـَيْنِ (accusative and genitive).
Sound m. plural: ـُونَ / ـِينَ. Sound f. plural: ـَات.
Broken plurals change the inside of the word: قَلْب → قُلُوب.
Sūrat ar-Raḥmān's refrain ends in a dual: rabbikumā, tukadhdhibān.

title: The three cases
body: A noun's ending changes with its job in the sentence. Nominative (marfūʿ) usually ends in -u: it is the subject or the predicate. Accusative (manṣūb) usually ends in -a: it is an object, or follows inna and her sisters. Genitive (majrūr) usually ends in -i: it follows a preposition or is the second term of an iḍāfa.

Duals and sound masculine plurals show case with letters instead: -ūna or -āni for the nominative, -īna or -ayni for the other two. Some nouns (mamnūʿ min aṣ-ṣarf, such as many proper names) take -a in the genitive and no tanwīn.
The case is how you check that you understand an āyah. In ٱلْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ, al-ḥamdu is nominative because it is the subject, and allāhi is genitive because it follows li-.
points: Marfūʿ -u / -ūna / -āni: subject, predicate.
Manṣūb -a / -īna / -ayni: object; noun after inna; predicate of kāna.
Majrūr -i / -īna / -ayni: after a preposition; second term of an iḍāfa.
Diptotes take -a for the genitive: إِلَىٰٓ إِبْرَٰهِيمَ (2:136).

title: The five nouns
body: Five common nouns show their case with a long vowel instead of a short one when they are the first term of an iḍāfa: أَبُو / أَبَا / أَبِى (father), أَخُو / أَخَا / أَخِى (brother), ذُو / ذَا / ذِى (possessor of), plus ḥamū (in-law) and fū (mouth).

Wāw marks the nominative, alif the accusative, yāʾ the genitive: ذُو ٱلْفَضْلِ ٱلْعَظِيمِ 'Possessor of great bounty' (nominative), and إِلَىٰٓ أَبِيهِمْ 'to their father' (genitive). Dhū is how the Quran builds many of God's descriptions.
points: abū / abā / abī: -ū nominative, -ā accusative, -ī genitive.
Only when they are muḍāf (first term of an iḍāfa).
dhū = possessor of: ذُو ٱلْعَرْشِ, ذِى ٱلْقُرْبَىٰ.
With 'my' (-ī) the long vowel does not show: أَبِى, أَخِى.

title: Attached pronouns
body: Pronoun endings attach to nouns (to mean 'my, your, his'), to verbs (as objects) and to prepositions. The core set is: ـِي/ـنِي (me, my), ـنَا (us, our), ـكَ (you m.), ـكِ (you f.), ـكُمْ (you m. pl.), ـهُ (him, his), ـهَا (her), ـهُمْ (them m.), ـهُنَّ (them f.), and the duals ـكُمَا and ـهُمَا.
After i or y, ـهُ, ـهُمْ and ـهُنَّ change to ـهِ, ـهِمْ and ـهِنَّ: فِيهِ, عَلَيْهِمْ. In the mushaf a small wāw or yāʾ after ـهُۥ marks a lengthened vowel.
points: ـهُ his/him, ـهَا her, ـهُمْ their (m.), ـهُنَّ their (f.).
ـكَ your (m.), ـكُمْ your (pl.), ـنَا our, ـِي my.
ـنِي = me after verbs: ذَرْنِى (74:11), ٱدْعُونِىٓ (40:60).
ـهِ after i/y: بِهِۦ, عَلَيْهِ.

title: Separate pronouns and demonstratives
body: Separate pronouns stand alone: أَنَا I, نَحْنُ we, أَنتَ you (m.), أَنتُمْ you (pl.), هُوَ he, هِيَ she, هُمْ they. In the Quran, إِيَّاكَ is the object form that comes before the verb for emphasis, as in إِيَّاكَ نَعْبُدُ, 'You alone we worship'.

Demonstratives point. هَـٰذَا (this, m.), هَـٰذِهِۦ (this, f.), and هَـٰٓؤُلَآءِ (these) are near. ذَٰلِكَ (that, m.), تِلْكَ (that, f.), and أُو۟لَـٰٓئِكَ (those) are far. ذَٰلِكَ ٱلْكِتَـٰبُ 'that Book' uses the far form for the Quran to mark its rank.
points: huwa, hiya, hum, hunna; anta, anti, antum; anā, naḥnu.
iyyā- + suffix = object put first: iyyāka naʿbudu.
Near: hādhā, hādhihi, hāʾulāʾi. Far: dhālika, tilka, ulāʾika.
Pronouns and demonstratives count as nouns (asmāʾ).

title: Relative pronouns
body: Relative pronouns join a clause to a noun, like 'who' and 'which'. ٱلَّذِى (m. sing.), ٱلَّتِى (f. sing.), ٱلَّذِينَ (m. pl., the most frequent), and ٱللَّـٰتِى / ٱلَّـٰٓئِى (f. pl.). مَن means 'whoever, the one who' for persons, and مَا means 'what, that which' for things.
The clause after it (ṣila) must contain a pronoun that refers back. In ٱلَّذِينَ يُؤْمِنُونَ بِٱلْغَيْبِ 'those who believe in the unseen', the referring pronoun is the -ūna inside the verb.
points: alladhī, allatī, alladhīna, allātī.
man = who (persons), mā = what (things).
Alladhīna is among the most frequent words in the Quran, so learn it early.
The clause after it needs a pronoun pointing back.

title: Prepositions
body: A preposition (ḥarf jarr) always puts the noun after it in the genitive. Some are separate words: مِنْ min (from), إِلَى ilā (to), عَنْ ʿan (away from), عَلَى ʿalā (on), فِي fī (in). Others are one letter joined to the noun: بِـ bi- (with or by), لِـ li- (for or belonging to), كَـ ka- (like). وَ wa- is also used to swear an oath, as in وَٱلْعَصْرِ 'by the time'.
A preposition and its noun (jārr wa-majrūr) often come before what they describe, for emphasis or rhyme: لِلَّهِ ٱلْأَمْرُ 'to God belongs the command'.
points: min, ilā, ʿan, ʿalā, fī, bi-, li-, ka-, ḥattā, wa- of oath.
The noun after a preposition is always majrūr.
li- + al- is written لِلْ, so lil-muttaqīn.
An oath with wa- or ta-: وَٱلشَّمْسِ, تَٱللَّهِ.

title: The possessive construction (iḍāfa)
body: Two nouns side by side can mean 'the X of Y': رَبِّ ٱلْعَـٰلَمِينَ 'Lord of the worlds', يَوْمِ ٱلدِّينِ 'the Day of Judgement'. The first term (muḍāf) never takes al- or tanwīn. Its case depends on its job in the sentence. The second term (muḍāf ilayhi) is always genitive.
If the second term is definite, the whole phrase is definite. Attached pronouns work the same way: رَبُّكَ 'your Lord' is an iḍāfa of rabb and -ka.
points: Muḍāf: no al-, no tanwīn, any case.
Muḍāf ilayhi: always genitive.
A chain is possible: بِسْمِ ٱللَّهِ, 'in the name of God'.
Noun + pronoun suffix is also an iḍāfa: كِتَـٰبَهُۥ.

title: Participles
body: The active participle (ism fāʿil) names the doer. In Form I it is fāʿil: kāfir (one who covers or denies), ʿālim (one who knows), ṣābir (patient). In the derived forms it begins with mu- and has i before the last letter: muʾmin (believer, IV), muttaqī (one who is mindful, VIII), muslim (IV).

The passive participle (ism mafʿūl) names what is acted on. In Form I it is mafʿūl: maghḍūb (one on whom anger falls), maktūb (written). In the derived forms it is mu- with a before the last letter: munzal (sent down).
points: Form I: fāʿil (doer) / mafʿūl (done to).
Derived forms: mu-…-i- (doer) / mu-…-a- (done to): mukram vs mukrim.
Participles are nouns: they take case, al- and tanwīn.
Al-maghḍūbi ʿalayhim and aḍ-ḍāllīn: a passive then an active participle (1:7).

title: The past tense
body: The past (māḍī) is the base form of the verb: فَعَلَ 'he did'. Person is shown by endings: فَعَلَتْ she did, فَعَلُوا۟ they did, فَعَلْتَ you (m.) did, فَعَلْتُمْ you (pl.) did, فَعَلْتُ I did, فَعَلْنَا we did.
The Quran often uses the past for events that are certain but still to come, especially the Hour: إِذَا ٱلسَّمَآءُ ٱنفَطَرَتْ 'when the sky is split open'. After idhā, read the past as a future.
points: Base: faʿala (he). -at she, -ū they, -ta you, -tum you all, -tu I, -nā we.
A past verb after idhā or in a condition often means the future.
Qad + past = 'has already': قَدْ أَفْلَحَ.
The Quran's most frequent verb is qāla, 'he said'.

title: The present tense
body: The present (muḍāriʿ) adds a prefix from the letters أ ن ي ت. يَفْعَلُ he does, تَفْعَلُ she does or you do, أَفْعَلُ I do, نَفْعَلُ we do. Plurals add ـُونَ: يَفْعَلُونَ they do, تَفْعَلُونَ you all do.

It covers present and future, and sa- or sawfa make the future explicit: سَيَعْلَمُونَ 'they will come to know'. The very frequent closing of āyāt, لَعَلَّكُمْ تَتَّقُونَ, uses it: 'so that you may be mindful'.
points: Prefixes: ya- he/they, ta- she/you, a- I, na- we.
-ūna for the plural, -āni for the dual, -īna for 'you (f. sing.)'.
sa- / sawfa = will.
The default ending is -u (indicative); Lesson 17 explains -a and the dropped endings.

title: Commands and prohibitions
body: The command (amr) is formed from the present by dropping the prefix and adding a helping vowel when needed: تَقْرَأُ → ٱقْرَأْ 'Read!'. قُلْ 'Say!' is the most frequent command in the Quran. Plural commands end in ـُوا۟: ٱعْبُدُوا۟.
A prohibition is lā + the jussive present: لَا تَحْزَنْ 'do not grieve'. Many duʿāʾs in the Quran are commands addressed to God in humility: رَبِّ ٱغْفِرْ لِى.
points: Amr: drop the prefix, keep sukūn: ٱقْرَأْ, قُلْ, ٱصْبِرْ.
Plural amr: ٱعْبُدُوا۟, ٱتَّقُوا۟.
Prohibition: lā + majzūm: لَا تَقْرَبُوا۟.
Qul ('Say') opens five sūrahs.

title: The five verbs
body: Present-tense verbs that end in -ūna, -āni or -īna (they, you all, the two of them, you f.) are 'the five verbs'. Their indicative keeps the final nūn: يَعْلَمُونَ, تُكَذِّبَانِ.
In the subjunctive and jussive the nūn drops: لَمْ يَعْلَمُوا۟, أَن تَقُولُوا۟. A dropped nūn plus a silent alif (ـُوا۟) is the sign to look for when you meet lam, lan or an.
points: yafʿalūna, tafʿalūna, yafʿalāni, tafʿalāni, tafʿalīna.
Indicative keeps the nūn.
Subjunctive and jussive drop it: lan tafʿalū, lam yafʿalū.
The silent alif after -ū (ـُوا۟) is written but not read.

title: Moods of the present
body: The present tense has three moods. The indicative (marfūʿ, -u, -ūna) is the default. The subjunctive (manṣūb, -a, and the -na of plurals drops) follows an (to), lan (will never), li- or kay (so that), and ḥattā (until): لَن تَرَىٰنِى 'you will never see Me'.

The jussive (majzūm, sukūn, plurals drop the -na) follows lam (did not), lā of prohibition, the li- of command, and the verbs of a condition: لَمْ يَلِدْ وَلَمْ يُولَدْ 'He did not beget and was not begotten'.
points: Marfūʿ: yafʿalu / yafʿalūna.
Manṣūb after an, lan, li-, kay, ḥattā: yafʿala / yafʿalū.
Majzūm after lam, lā (prohibition), in (if): yafʿal / yafʿalū.
Lam + jussive = a past negative: lam yalid.

title: Scales and the six patterns of Form I
body: Morphologists weigh every word on the scale ف ع ل. kataba is on the scale faʿala, its present yaktubu on yafʿulu. Form I verbs fall into six patterns (abwāb) according to the middle vowel in the past and present: faʿala–yafʿulu (naṣara–yanṣuru), faʿala–yafʿilu (ḍaraba–yaḍribu), faʿala–yafʿalu (fataḥa–yaftaḥu), faʿila–yafʿalu (ʿalima–yaʿlamu), faʿula–yafʿulu (karuma–yakrumu), faʿila–yafʿilu (ḥasiba–yaḥsibu).

The middle vowel is part of the word and must be learned with the verb, as your sarf books drill: qatala yaqtulu, jalasa yajlisu, ʿalima yaʿlamu. The Quran attests each verb in only some of its forms; the Words tab shows which ones.
points: Scale: ف ع ل stand for the three root letters.
naṣara/yanṣuru, ḍaraba/yaḍribu, fataḥa/yaftaḥu.
ʿalima/yaʿlamu, karuma/yakrumu, ḥasiba/yaḥsibu.
Learn each verb as a pair: past + present.

title: Sound and weak verbs
body: Sarf sorts roots into types. Ṣaḥīḥ (sound): no weak letter, hamza or doubling, as in ك ت ب. Mahmūz: contains a hamza (أ م ن, س أ ل, ق ر أ). Muḍāʿaf: second and third letters are the same (م د د, ض ل ل).

Weak (muʿtall) roots contain و or ي: mithāl if it is the first letter (و ع د), ajwaf (hollow) if it is the middle (ق و ل), nāqiṣ (defective) if it is the last (ه د ي, د ع و), and lafīf if there are two (و ق ي, ر و ي). Each type changes shape in its own predictable way.
points: ṣaḥīḥ: ك ت ب. mahmūz: hamza. muḍāʿaf: 2nd = 3rd letter.
mithāl: weak 1st (wa-ʿa-da). ajwaf: weak 2nd (qā-la).
nāqiṣ: weak 3rd (ha-dā). lafīf: two weak letters (wa-qā).
The type tells you how the verb will bend.

title: Weak roots
body: Roots containing و or ي (and sometimes hamza) change shape. Hollow verbs (middle weak) show a long ā in the past: qāla 'he said' from q-w-l, and in the present yaqūlu. With a consonant ending the vowel shortens: qultu, and the command is qul.

Defective verbs (last weak) end in a vowel: hadā 'he guided' (h-d-y), yahdī, and the command ihdi, as in ٱهْدِنَا. Assimilated verbs (first weak) drop the w in the present: waʿada → yaʿidu. Finding the hidden root is the key skill. The Roots drill trains it on your own āyāt.
points: Hollow: qāla / yaqūlu / qul (q-w-l); jāʾa / yajīʾu (j-y-ʾ).
Defective: hadā / yahdī / ihdi (h-d-y); daʿā / yadʿū (d-ʿ-w).
Assimilated: waʿada / yaʿidu (w-ʿ-d).
When a letter seems missing, try و or ي in that slot.

title: Derived forms II to IV
body: From one root, Arabic builds up to ten verb forms. Form I is the simple verb, faʿala. Form II, faʿʿala, doubles the middle letter and often makes the action intensive or causative: ʿalima 'he knew' → ʿallama 'he taught'. Form III, fāʿala, adds an ā and often means doing something with or to someone: jāhada 'he strove'.
Form IV, afʿala, adds an initial a- and usually makes the verb causative: nazala 'came down' → anzala 'sent down'; āmana 'believed' (from a-m-n). Its present has u on the prefix: yuʾminu, yunzilu.
points: II faʿʿala / yufaʿʿilu: ʿallama, kadhdhaba, nazzala.
III fāʿala / yufāʿilu: jāhada, qātala.
IV afʿala / yufʿilu: anzala, aslama, āmana.
Forms II to IV have u on the present prefix: yu-.

title: Derived forms V to X
body: Form V, tafaʿʿala, is often reflexive of II: tadhakkara 'he took heed'. Form VI, tafāʿala, is often mutual: tasāʾala 'they asked one another'. Form VII, infaʿala, is often passive in meaning: infaṭara 'was split'.

Form VIII, iftaʿala, puts a t after the first root letter: ittaqā 'was mindful' (from w-q-y), ikhtalafa 'differed'. Form X, istafʿala, often means seeking: istaghfara 'sought forgiveness', istaʿāna 'sought help' (as in nastaʿīn, Al-Fātiḥa).
points: V tafaʿʿala (tadhakkara), VI tafāʿala (tasāʾala).
VII infaʿala (infaṭara, inshaqqa): passive or reflexive.
VIII iftaʿala (ittaqā, ikhtalafa, ihtadā).
X istafʿala (istaghfara, istaʿāna, istakbara): seeking or deeming.

title: The verbal noun
body: The maṣdar names the action itself: ʿilm (knowing, knowledge), ṣabr (patience), hudā (guidance), raḥma (mercy). In Form I its patterns vary and must be learned. In the derived forms they are regular: II tafʿīl (tanzīl, 'sending down'), III mufāʿala or fiʿāl (jihād), IV ifʿāl (islām, īmān), VIII iftiʿāl, X istifʿāl (istighfār).
Many of the Quran's key terms are maṣdars: īmān, islām, iḥsān, taqwā, ṣalāh, zakāh.
points: Form I maṣdar varies: ʿilm, ṣabr, dhikr, rizq.
II tafʿīl, IV ifʿāl, V tafaʿʿul, VIII iftiʿāl, X istifʿāl.
īmān and islām are Form IV maṣdars of āmana and aslama.
A maṣdar after its own verb gives emphasis: كَلَّمَ … تَكْلِيمًا.

title: Derived nouns
body: Beyond the participles, Arabic derives several noun shapes from a root. The elative afʿal means 'more / most': أَكْبَرُ greater, أَعْلَمُ more knowing, أَحْسَنُ best. The noun of place and time mafʿal / mafʿil names where or when: مَسْجِد place of prostration, مَشْرِق place of sunrise.

The noun of instrument mifʿāl / mifʿal names a tool: مِيزَان scale, مِصْبَاح lamp. The intensive faʿʿāl and faʿūl mean 'much given to': غَفَّار ever-forgiving, تَوَّاب ever-relenting, غَفُور most forgiving.
points: afʿal = more / most: akbar, aʿlam, aḥsan.
mafʿal / mafʿil = place or time: masjid, mashriq.
mifʿāl = instrument: mīzān, miṣbāḥ.
faʿʿāl / faʿūl = intensive: ghaffār, tawwāb, ghafūr.

title: The nominal sentence
body: A sentence that starts with a noun is nominal. Its subject (mubtadaʾ) and predicate (khabar) are both nominative, and Arabic needs no word for 'is'. ٱللَّهُ ٱلصَّمَدُ means 'God is the Eternal Refuge'. ٱلْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ means 'praise is to God'.

The predicate can be a noun, a prepositional phrase (لِلَّهِ) or a whole clause. When the predicate is a prepositional phrase and the subject is indefinite, the phrase comes first: لَهُمْ عَذَابٌ 'for them is a punishment'.
points: Mubtadaʾ + khabar, both marfūʿ, with no verb 'to be'.
The khabar can be a word, a jārr-majrūr phrase or a sentence.
Indefinite subject → predicate first: لَهُمْ عَذَابٌ أَلِيمٌ.
Kāna and inna change the cases (Lesson 23).

title: Inna, kāna and their sisters
body: Inna ('indeed') and her sisters (anna 'that', lākinna 'but', kaʾanna 'as if', layta 'if only', laʿalla 'perhaps, so that') enter a nominal sentence and make the subject accusative while the predicate stays nominative: إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ غَفُورٌ رَّحِيمٌ.

Kāna ('was') and her sisters (aṣbaḥa, ẓalla, ṣāra, laysa 'is not', mā zāla 'still') do the opposite. The subject stays nominative and the predicate becomes accusative: وَكَانَ ٱللَّهُ عَلِيمًا حَكِيمًا, 'and God is ever Knowing, Wise'. Commentators read kāna here as 'ever so', not merely 'was'.
points: Inna + ism manṣūb + khabar marfūʿ.
Kāna + ism marfūʿ + khabar manṣūb.
Sisters of inna: anna, lākinna, kaʾanna, layta, laʿalla.
Sisters of kāna: aṣbaḥa, amsā, ẓalla, bāta, ṣāra, laysa, mā zāla.

title: Ẓanna and her sisters
body: Verbs of thinking and making (ẓanna 'thought', ḥasiba 'reckoned', ʿalima 'knew', raʾā 'saw, judged', jaʿala 'made') enter a nominal sentence and make both of its parts accusative: they take two objects.
أَيَحْسَبُ ٱلْإِنسَـٰنُ أَن يُتْرَكَ سُدًى 'Does man think he will be left to no purpose?' Here an-clause stands in for the two objects, a common pattern after ḥasiba and ẓanna.
points: ẓanna, ḥasiba, khāla, zaʿama: verbs of opinion.
ʿalima, raʾā, wajada: verbs of certainty.
jaʿala, ṣayyara, ittakhadha: verbs of making.
Both objects are manṣūb, or an an-/anna-clause replaces them.

title: The verbal sentence
body: A sentence that starts with a verb is verbal. Its doer (fāʿil) is nominative and its object (mafʿūl bihi) accusative: خَلَقَ ٱللَّهُ ٱلسَّمَـٰوَٰتِ 'God created the heavens' (as-samāwāti is accusative; sound feminine plurals take -i for the accusative).

When the doer is a noun after the verb, the verb stays singular even for a plural doer: قَالَ ٱلْمَلَأُ 'the chiefs said'. When there is no separate noun, the doer is the pronoun inside the verb: قَالُوا۟ 'they said'.
points: fiʿl + fāʿil (marfūʿ) + mafʿūl bihi (manṣūb).
A verb before a plural noun stays singular: qāla l-malaʾu.
The doer can be hidden in the verb's ending.
An object can come first for emphasis: إِيَّاكَ نَعْبُدُ.

title: The passive voice
body: The passive hides the doer. In the past, the first vowel becomes u and the second i: نَزَلَ → أُنزِلَ 'was sent down'. In the present, the prefix takes u and the vowel before the last letter becomes a: يُنفَخُ 'is blown'.

The Quran uses the passive when the doer is obvious (God) or beside the point: وَإِذَا ٱلْجِبَالُ سُيِّرَتْ 'and when the mountains are set in motion'. The noun that would have been the object becomes the subject and takes the nominative (nāʾib al-fāʿil).
points: Past passive: fuʿila (u…i): خُلِقَ, قُتِلَ, أُنزِلَ.
Present passive: yufʿalu (u…a): يُنفَخُ, يُقَالُ.
The former object becomes marfūʿ.
Juz ʿAmma's scenes of the Hour use many passives: سُجِّرَتْ, نُشِرَتْ.

title: The other accusatives
ar: المنصوبات: المفعول المطلق والحال والتمييز والمفعول لأجله
body: Besides the object, four more jobs make a noun accusative, and Safina's book teaches them together. The absolute object (mafʿūl muṭlaq) is the verb's own maṣdar, for emphasis or manner: وَرَتِّلِ ٱلْقُرْءَانَ تَرْتِيلًا 'and recite the Quran with measured recitation'.

The ḥāl tells the state of someone while the action happens: وَخُلِقَ ٱلْإِنسَـٰنُ ضَعِيفًا 'man was created weak'. The tamyīz clears up what is meant after a vague word or number: وَٱشْتَعَلَ ٱلرَّأْسُ شَيْبًا 'the head has blazed with white hair'. The mafʿūl li-ajlih gives the reason: خَشْيَةَ إِمْلَـٰقٍ 'for fear of poverty'.
points: mafʿūl muṭlaq: the verb's maṣdar: kallama … taklīman.
ḥāl: the state: usually indefinite, answers 'how?'.
tamyīz: specifies: 'in what respect?' after numbers, comparisons.
mafʿūl li-ajlih: the reason, often a maṣdar: ibtighāʾa, khashyata.

title: Followers: adjective, conjunction, emphasis, substitute
body: Four kinds of words 'follow' the word before them and copy its case. The adjective (naʿt) also copies its gender, number and definiteness: ٱلصِّرَٰطَ ٱلْمُسْتَقِيمَ. A noun joined by wa or fa (ʿaṭf) takes the same case as the first.

Emphasis (tawkīd) repeats or uses words like kull and ajmaʿ: فَسَجَدَ ٱلْمَلَـٰٓئِكَةُ كُلُّهُمْ أَجْمَعُونَ 'so the angels prostrated, all of them together'. The substitute (badal) renames what came before: صِرَٰطَ ٱلَّذِينَ in Al-Fātiḥah restates 'the straight path' as 'the path of those You have blessed'.
points: naʿt agrees in case, gender, number and definiteness.
maʿṭūf takes the case of what it is joined to.
tawkīd: kull, ajmaʿūn, nafs, ʿayn.
badal restates the noun before it, in the same case.

title: Call, oath and emphasis
body: yā calls someone: يَـٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلنَّاسُ 'O people'. Before a noun with al-, Arabic inserts ayyuhā (masc.) or ayyatuhā (fem.): يَـٰٓأَيَّتُهَا ٱلنَّفْسُ ٱلْمُطْمَئِنَّةُ. Duʿāʾs often drop yā: رَبَّنَا 'our Lord'.

Emphasis stacks. inna at the start, la- on the predicate, qad (certainly) before the past, and the energetic -anna on a verb: لَتُسْـَٔلُنَّ 'you will surely be asked'. Oaths (wa-, ta-) are answered by an emphasised sentence: وَٱلْعَصْرِ ۝ إِنَّ ٱلْإِنسَـٰنَ لَفِى خُسْرٍ.
points: yā ayyuhā + al-noun.
rabbanā = (O) our Lord, with yā dropped.
inna … la- = double emphasis.
Energetic ending -anna / -an: لَنَسْفَعًۢا.

title: Negation
body: Arabic has a negative for each time and type. lā + present = does not: لَا يَعْلَمُونَ. mā + past = did not: مَا وَدَّعَكَ رَبُّكَ. lam + jussive = did not (very common): لَمْ يَلِدْ. lan + subjunctive = will never: لَن تَنَالُوا۟.
laysa negates a nominal sentence ('is not'): لَيْسَ لَهَا مِن دُونِ ٱللَّهِ كَاشِفَةٌ. in + illā means 'only' or 'nothing but': إِنْ هُوَ إِلَّا ذِكْرٌ 'it is nothing but a reminder'.
points: lā + muḍāriʿ = does not; lā + jussive = do not!
mā + māḍī = did not; lam + jussive = did not.
lan + manṣūb = will never.
in … illā / mā … illā = nothing but.

title: Adverbs of time and place
body: Adverbs (ẓarf) answer 'when?' and 'where?': yawma (on the day), ḥīna (when, at the time), qabla (before), baʿda (after), ʿinda (with, at), fawqa (above), taḥta (beneath), bayna (between), amāma (in front).
They are accusative or built on a fixed ending, and they usually take the next noun in the genitive as an iḍāfa: يَوْمَ ٱلْقِيَـٰمَةِ, تَحْتِهَا ٱلْأَنْهَـٰرُ. idh, idhā and ḥaythu are fixed adverbs.
points: Time: yawma, ḥīna, qabla, baʿda, idh, idhā.
Place: ʿinda, fawqa, taḥta, bayna, ḥaythu, ladā.
The noun after them is genitive.
tajrī min taḥtihā l-anhār: one of the Quran's commonest phrases.

title: Exception
body: Exception uses illā (except) and words like ghayr and siwā. In a complete positive sentence the excepted noun is accusative: فَسَجَدُوٓا۟ إِلَّآ إِبْلِيسَ 'so they prostrated, except Iblīs'.

After a negative, illā means 'only' and the noun takes whatever case the sentence needs: لَآ إِلَـٰهَ إِلَّا ٱللَّهُ 'there is no god except God'. This restriction is the strongest way Arabic says 'only'.
points: illā = except; ghayr / siwā + genitive = other than.
Positive + illā: the excepted noun is manṣūb.
Negative + illā = 'only, nothing but'.
lā ilāha illā llāh: negation + exception = restriction.

title: Conditions and time
body: in ('if') and man ('whoever') introduce a condition, and both verbs go into the jussive: وَمَن يَتَوَكَّلْ عَلَى ٱللَّهِ فَهُوَ حَسْبُهُۥ. law means 'if (it were the case)', for unreal conditions. The answer clause often begins with fa- or la-.

idhā ('when') is a time word that looks to a certain future. Sūrahs 81, 82, 84 and 99 open with chains of idhā clauses about the Hour, whose answer comes after the chain. In Sūrah 81 it is عَلِمَتْ نَفْسٌ مَّآ أَحْضَرَتْ (81:14).
points: in / man + jussive … fa-answer.
law + past … la-answer: unreal condition.
idhā + past = 'when (it will happen)'.
idh = 'when (it happened)': the start of many stories.

title: Joining: wa, fa and thumma
body: wa- 'and' joins with no sense of order. fa- 'so, then' joins with immediate sequence or result: فَصَلِّ لِرَبِّكَ وَٱنْحَرْ 'so pray to your Lord and sacrifice'. thumma 'then, later' adds a gap in time or rank. aw is 'or', bal 'rather'.
The Quran also uses wa- and fa- to begin a new sentence (resumption). The corpus tags these 'REM'. That is why so many āyāt start with و or ف.
points: wa = and; fa = so / and then (right away); thumma = then (later).
aw = or; am = or (in questions); bal = rather.
Joined nouns share the same case.
fa- also opens the answer to a condition.

title: Numbers
body: Numbers 3 to 10 take the opposite gender of the counted noun, which follows in the genitive plural: سَبْعَ سَمَـٰوَٰتٍ 'seven heavens' (samāʾ is feminine, so sabʿ has no tāʾ), ثَمَـٰنِيَةَ أَيَّامٍ 'eight days'.

Eleven to ninety-nine take the counted noun in the accusative singular, as a tamyīz: أَحَدَ عَشَرَ كَوْكَبًا 'eleven stars', ٱثْنَا عَشَرَ شَهْرًا 'twelve months'. Hundreds and thousands take the genitive singular.
points: 1 and 2 agree with the noun; 3–10 take the opposite gender.
3–10 + genitive plural: sabʿa samāwātin.
11–99 + accusative singular: aḥada ʿashara kawkaban.
100 / 1000 + genitive singular: alfa sanatin.

title: Seeking refuge and the basmala
body: Tajwīd means 'making excellent': giving every letter its due when reciting. Knowing its rules is a communal duty, but reciting al-Fātiḥah correctly is a personal duty on every Muslim. Recite knowing these are the words of God, not of any created being.

Begin with the istiʿādha, aʿūdhu billāhi mina sh-shayṭāni r-rajīm: aloud if you recite aloud, silently if you read silently. Recite the basmala before every sūrah except at-Tawbah. Between two sūrahs you may join all three parts or pause between them, but never join the end of one sūrah to the basmala and then stop before the next.
points: Istiʿādha before reciting; basmala before every sūrah except at-Tawbah.
Between sūrahs: join all, pause after each, or stop then join basmala + sūrah.
Not allowed: end of sūrah + basmala, then a stop.
A long break (talk) means saying the istiʿādha again; a cough or sneeze does not.
qs: Before which sūrah is the basmala not recited?
Between two sūrahs, which way of reciting is NOT allowed?
Join the end of the sūrah to the basmala, then stop before the next sūrah
Stop after the sūrah and after the basmala
Stop after the sūrah, then join the basmala to the next sūrah
Reciting al-Fātiḥah with correct tajwīd is…
A personal duty on every Muslim

title: Silent letters: waṣl and lām shamsiyya
body: Some letters are written but not read. The hamzat al-waṣl (ٱ) is heard only when you start on it; joined to the word before, it falls silent: bismi llāhi, not bismi allāhi. The lām of al- before a sun letter is silent and the next letter doubles: ٱلشَّمْسِ ash-shams.
The mushaf also writes letters that are never read, such as the alif after the -ū of a plural verb: قَالُوا۟. The small circle (۟) above them is the sign: skip the letter.
points: ٱ is silent when joined; at the start of a recitation it is read a / i / u.
Lām shamsiyya: silent lām, doubled next letter.
Lām qamariyya: lām with sukūn is heard: ٱلْقَمَرِ.
A letter with ۟ over it is not pronounced.
qs: silent, and the shīn is doubled

title: Where the letters come from
body: Correct letters come first. ḥāʾ (ح) and ʿayn (ع) come from the middle of the throat; khāʾ (خ) and ghayn (غ) from its nearest part, ghayn like a gargle; hāʾ (ه) and hamza (ء) from its deepest part, almost the chest. A final hāʾ is breathed out audibly.

Thāʾ (ث) and dhāl (ذ) put the tongue between the teeth; dhāl buzzes, unlike zāy. Ṭāʾ and tāʾ must be dry, with no whistle. Ḍād (ض), the hardest letter, uses the side of the tongue against the molars; Arabic is called 'the language of the ḍād'. Sīn smiles; ṣād opens the mouth vertically; kāf comes from the tongue just ahead of qāf, which is deeper. Rāʾ is one light tap, neither English r nor a trill.
points: Middle throat: ح ع. Nearest throat: خ غ. Deepest: ء ه.
Between the teeth: ث ذ ظ.
ض: side of the tongue against the molars.
ق deeper than ك; ر is a single tap.
qs: Which two letters come from the deepest part of the throat?
Which letter is pronounced with the side of the tongue against the molars?
the nearest part of the throat
a single light tap of the tongue
Which letter is called the hardest in the language?

title: Whisper and bounce: hams and qalqala
body: Ten letters carry hams, a breath that escapes when they have sukūn: the phrase فَحَثَّهُ شَخْصٌ سَكَتَ gathers them. Hold their sukūn slightly with that breath.

Five letters bounce when they have sukūn: qalqala, gathered in قُطْبُ جَدٍّ (ق ط ب ج د). In the middle of a word the bounce is small (ṣughrā); at the end of a word, and above all when you stop on it, it is strongest (kubrā): أَحَدْ, ٱلْفَلَقْ.
points: Hams letters: فحثه شخص سكت (breath escapes).
Qalqala letters: قطب جد.
Ṣughrā: in the middle of a word: يَجْعَلُونَ.
Kubrā: at the end, especially when stopping: أَحَدْ.
qs: Which phrase gathers the qalqala letters?
Qalqala on a letter at the end of the word when stopping is…

title: Heavy and light letters
body: Seven letters are always heavy (mufakhkham), the letters of istiʿlāʾ: خُصَّ ضَغْطٍ قِظْ (خ ص ض غ ط ق ظ). An alif after one of them is heavy too, as in ٱلضَّآلِّينَ; after any other letter it is light, as in مَآءٍ.

Rāʾ is heavy by default: with fatḥa or ḍamma, رَبِّ, ٱلرُّسُلُ. It is light in three cases: when it has a kasra (رِجَالٌ); when it has sukūn after a kasra (أَنذِرْ); when it has sukūn after a sukūn letter that follows a kasra (حِجْرٌ, when stopping).
points: Always heavy: خص ضغط قظ.
Alif follows the letter before it.
Rāʾ heavy with fatḥa or ḍamma; light with kasra.
Rāʾ sākina is light after a kasra: firʿawn, unḏhir.
qs: Which phrase gathers the always-heavy letters?

title: The natural madd
body: A long vowel letter (alif after fatḥa, wāw after ḍamma, yāʾ after kasra) is held for two counts: this is madd ṭabīʿī, the natural length. The dagger alif (ـٰ) is held the same way: مَـٰلِكِ.
If a natural madd is followed by a hamzat al-waṣl, it is dropped when you join: فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ is read fi l-arḍ.
points: Alif after fatḥa, wāw after ḍamma, yāʾ after kasra: 2 counts.
Dagger alif ـٰ: also 2 counts.
Dropped before a joined hamzat al-waṣl.
The baseline every other madd is measured against.
qs: How long is the natural madd?

title: Madd before a hamza
body: When a madd letter is followed by a hamza in the same word, it is madd muttaṣil (connected) and must be held four to five counts: جَآءَ, ٱلسَّمَآءِ. The mushaf marks it with a wavy line (ٓ).
When the hamza begins the next word, it is madd munfaṣil (separated), held four or five counts in Ḥafṣ by way of ash-Shāṭibiyya: إِنَّآ أَعْطَيْنَـٰكَ, فَلَمَّآ أَضَآءَتْ.
points: Muttaṣil: madd + hamza in the same word: 4–5.
Munfaṣil: madd, then hamza in the next word: 4–5.
Both are marked with ٓ in the mushaf.
Keep the same length throughout one recitation.
qs: muttaṣil: the hamza is in the same word

title: Madd lāzim, līn and ʿāriḍ
body: Madd lāzim (obligatory) is a madd letter followed by a permanent sukūn or shadda: ٱلضَّآلِّينَ, and the opening letters such as الٓمٓ. It is always six counts.

When you stop at the end of an āyah, the last vowel becomes sukūn. A madd letter just before it becomes madd ʿāriḍ lil-sukūn, held two, four or six counts: نَسْتَعِينْ. If the letter before is wāw or yāʾ with sukūn after a fatḥa, it is madd līn, as in every āyah-end of Sūrat Quraysh: قُرَيْشْ, ٱلصَّيْفْ, ٱلْبَيْتْ, خَوْفْ.
points: Lāzim: madd + permanent sukūn or shadda: 6 counts.
ʿĀriḍ lil-sukūn: madd before a stop: 2, 4 or 6.
Līn: fatḥa + و or ي with sukūn, before a stop.
Sūrat Quraysh ends every āyah with madd līn.
qs: Every āyah-end of Sūrat Quraysh has which madd when you stop?

title: Ṣila: the lengthened hāʾ
body: The pronoun hāʾ (-hu, -hi) at the end of a word, between two voweled letters, is lengthened two counts when you join it to the next word: after fatḥa or ḍamma it sounds like wāw, إِنَّهُۥ كَانَ; after kasra like yāʾ, بِهِۦ.
The mushaf shows ṣila with a small wāw (ۥ) or yāʾ (ۦ). If the next word starts with a hamza, it becomes four to five counts, like a munfaṣil: مَالَهُۥٓ أَخْلَدَهُۥ.
points: Ṣila: hāʾ al-kināya lengthened when joined: 2 counts.
After fatḥa/ḍamma → like wāw (ۥ).
After kasra → like yāʾ (ۦ).
Before a hamza → 4–5 counts.
qs: The small wāw in إِنَّهُۥ tells you to…
lengthen the hāʾ like a wāw when joining

title: Ghunna on doubled nūn and mīm
body: Ghunna is the humming sound from the nose. Every nūn or mīm with a shadda carries a full ghunna of two counts: إِنَّ, ثُمَّ, ٱلنَّاسِ.
The same nasal sound appears in idghām with ghunna, ikhfāʾ and iqlāb, which come next.
points: نّ and مّ: ghunna of 2 counts.
Ghunna comes from the nose.
Present in idghām bi-ghunna, ikhfāʾ, iqlāb.
Practise on إِنَّ, ثُمَّ, ٱلنَّاسِ.

title: Nūn sākina and tanwīn: iẓhār and ikhfāʾ
body: A nūn with sukūn or a tanwīn has four rules, depending on the next letter. Before the six throat letters (ء ه ع ح غ خ) it is pronounced clearly: iẓhār, as in إِنْ أَنتُمْ, سَوِيًّا عَلَىٰ. The mushaf usually shows this nūn with a visible sukūn.
Before fifteen letters (ت ث ج د ذ ز س ش ص ض ط ظ ف ق ك) it is hidden with a light nasal sound: ikhfāʾ, as in إِن كُنتُمْ, مِن قَبْلِكَ.
points: Iẓhār before ء ه ع ح غ خ: clear nūn.
Ikhfāʾ before the 15 other letters: nasal, hidden nūn.
Watch across words: tanwīn + next word counts too.
The coloured letters in Sabaq mark each ikhfāʾ.
qs: Before which letters is nūn sākina pronounced clearly (iẓhār)?
ء ه ع ح غ خ
ي ر م ل و ن
In مِن قَبْلِكَ the nūn is…

title: Idghām and iqlāb
body: Before the letters of يَرْمَلُونَ (ي ر م ل و ن), nūn sākina and tanwīn merge into the next letter: idghām. Into ي ن م و the merge keeps a ghunna: مَن يَقُولُ, خَيْرًا يَرَهُۥ. Into ل and ر there is no ghunna: مِن لَّدُنْهُ, غَفُورٌ رَّحِيمٌ.
Before bāʾ, the nūn turns into a mīm with ghunna: iqlāb. The mushaf writes a small mīm (ۢ) above it: أَنۢبِئْهُم, عَلِيمٌۢ بِذَاتِ ٱلصُّدُورِ.
points: Idghām letters: يرملون.
With ghunna: ي ن م و. Without: ل ر.
Iqlāb: nūn + ب → mīm with ghunna (ۢ).
Idghām happens only across two words.
qs: Which word gathers the idghām letters?
Idghām into ل and ر is…

title: Mīm sākina
body: A mīm with sukūn has three rules. Before bāʾ it is hidden with ghunna: ikhfāʾ shafawī, تَرْمِيهِم بِحِجَارَةٍ. Before another mīm it merges with ghunna: idghām shafawī, ءَاذَانِهِم مِّنَ.
Before every other letter it is pronounced clearly: iẓhār shafawī, especially careful before wāw and fāʾ, which share its place at the lips: هُمْ فِيهَا, عَلَيْهِمْ وَلَا.
points: مْ + ب = ikhfāʾ shafawī (with ghunna).
مْ + م = idghām shafawī (with ghunna).
مْ + anything else = iẓhār shafawī.
Keep the mīm clear before و and ف.

title: Merging similar letters
body: When a letter with sukūn meets a letter that is the same or close to it, the first disappears into the second. Identical letters (mutamāthilayn): قُل لَّهُمْ, the two lāms merge. Letters from the same place (mutajānisayn): قَد تَّبَيَّنَ, dāl into tāʾ; also يَلْهَث ذَّٰلِكَ.
Close letters (mutaqāribayn): وَقُل رَّبِّ, lām into rāʾ, and أَلَمْ نَخْلُقكُّم, qāf into kāf.
points: Mutamāthilayn: same letter: قُل لَّهُمْ.
Mutajānisayn: same makhraj: قَد تَّبَيَّنَ.
Mutaqāribayn: close makhraj: قُل رَّبِّ.
The shadda on the second letter is the clue.
qs: In قُل لَّهُمْ the merge is…

title: Pause marks
body: The small marks above the line guide where to stop. ۘ (mīm) means a necessary stop: stopping elsewhere could change the meaning. ۙ (lā) means do not stop here. ۖ (ṣlā) means continuing is better; ۗ (qlā) means stopping is better; ۚ (jīm) means either is fine.
ۛ (three dots) comes in pairs: stop at one of them, never both: ذَٰلِكَ ٱلْكِتَـٰبُ لَا رَيْبَ ۛ فِيهِ ۛ هُدًى.
points: ۘ necessary stop; ۙ do not stop.
ۖ better to continue; ۗ better to stop.
ۚ either; ۛ stop at one of the pair.
At the end of an āyah, stopping is the Sunnah.
qs: Three dots ۛ in a pair mean…
stop at one of them, not both

title: All the rules together
body: Safina's book ends with practice on Juz ʿAmma: name the rule at each marked place. This lesson does the same on your own āyāt. Every coloured letter you met belongs to one of the rules above.
points: Madd: ṭabīʿī 2, muttaṣil/munfaṣil 4–5, lāzim 6, ʿāriḍ 2–6.
Nūn: iẓhār, idghām (±ghunna), iqlāb, ikhfāʾ.
Mīm: ikhfāʾ, idghām, iẓhār shafawī.
Qalqala: ṣughrā mid-word, kubrā at the end.
